title: Emergency Response

jokes.text: DYNAMITE stands for daring, youth-friendly, natural, amazing, merry, inviting, tourist attraction-y, and eco-friendly.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents an acronym for DYNAMITE as a summary of her park plan, clearly having forced the word to work.
jokes.punchline: 'Tourist attraction-y' and 'eco-friendly' as the final letters — the acronym is hilariously strained, especially 'tourist attraction-y' as a made-up adjectival form.
jokes.explanation: Pure Leslie Knope — the obsessive over-preparation, the forced acronym, the pride in something objectively absurd. 'Tourist attraction-y' is genuinely funny as a made-up word shoehorned into a governmental presentation. Strong character integration; only Leslie would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can sum up Pawnee Commons in one word: Dynamite.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: D-Y-N-A-M-I-T-E. Dynamic. Young. Nostalgic. Aspirational. Modern. Innovative. Tourist attraction-y. Exciting.

jokes.text: Thank you, Councilwoman Knope — very, very thorough and so many acronyms.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just delivered an elaborate DYNAMITE acronym presentation.
jokes.punchline: 'So many acronyms' — a deadpan acknowledgment of Leslie's excess, delivered with exhausted politeness.
jokes.explanation: A nice straight-man reaction that amplifies the absurdity of joke #1. Works as a button but is fairly routine sitcom structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: There was a standing ovation for my presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No there wasn't.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Everyone was sitting down the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: History will decide.

jokes.text: Let the record show there was a standing ovation. / No, there wasn't. / There was not. / History will decide.
jokes.setup: Jamm thanks everyone and says 'please be seated' as if there was a standing ovation.
jokes.punchline: Two people immediately and flatly deny it happened. Jamm's undeterred response: 'History will decide.'
jokes.explanation: Economical and perfectly constructed. The two-person simultaneous denial is funny, but 'History will decide' is the real gem — an absurdly grandiose claim from a petty local politician who just described a burger pitch. Highly quotable and very Jamm. Earns its 8 by having a great three-beat structure and strong character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Okay, here's my plan for the lot. We sell it to a developer. Developer builds luxury condos. People buy the condos. They live in the condos. It's a win for the developer, a win for the people living in the condos, a win for the city because of increased tax revenue, and a win for me because I facilitated the deal.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Quadruple-win.

jokes.text: My plan for lot 48 is simple. But why read it when you can shove it right in your face?
jokes.setup: Jamm begins his presentation as if he's making a sophisticated pitch.
jokes.punchline: 'Shove it right in your face' — an accidental vulgarity that reveals the crassness beneath the bravado.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's unintentional crudeness while trying to sound professional is good character comedy. The phrasing is genuinely odd enough to land.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: That's all I got.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: *drops mic*

jokes.text: We make money. They make money. They make burgers. We eat burgers. That's a win-win-win-win.
jokes.setup: Jamm presents his economic rationale for selling to Paunch Burger with mock seriousness.
jokes.punchline: The logic collapses into 'we eat burgers' as if it's an economic argument, capped by 'win-win-win-win' — four wins for a two-party transaction.
jokes.explanation: The escalating symmetry of 'we make money / they make money / they make burgers / we eat burgers' reads like parody business logic, and the extra 'wins' in the count is a precise, funny detail. Tight construction for a character comedy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not editorializing. That's literally what they call it. The Greasy Lard Bomb is their bestselling burger.

jokes.text: Are there curly fries? I love their curly fries.
jokes.setup: The commission has just heard an argument about community values vs. corporate fast food.
jokes.punchline: Ann's completely earnest, non-political response is to ask about curly fries.
jokes.explanation: Works as a deflating reaction beat — cutting through the political gravitas with mundane hunger. Leslie's 'Ann.' response (presumably a withering look) is the button.

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: You know what? Material possessions are forever. Love? Love fades. But this KitchenAid mixer? This will outlast your marriage. Guaranteed.

dialogue.speaker: Store Employee
dialogue.line: I've seen it a thousand times. Couples come in here all starry-eyed, pick out their china patterns, and then bam—six months later, he's gone. But that Cuisinart is still running strong.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm not editorializing. Paunch Burger's number-one-selling burger is the greasy lard bomb.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says the commission can choose between a 'beautiful, innovative community park or a bunch of greasy lard bombs,' then walks it back with 'I'm not editorializing.'
jokes.punchline: The actual product name IS 'The Greasy Lard Bomb,' making her technically correct.
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-constructed joke that rewards attention. The misdirection of apparent bias suddenly validated by absurd real-world fact is very Parks and Rec. The fictional Paunch Burger product name does heavy lifting in a single reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Did the Dalai Lama tell you that?

jokes.text: Love — love fades away. But things... Things are forever.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to pump up Ben and Ann about wedding registry shopping.
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'inspirational' quote is a consumerist inversion of romantic clichés — love is disposable, stuff is eternal. Delivered as if it's profound wisdom.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Tom's shallow materialism dressed up as romantic philosophy is a perfect encapsulation of the character. The rhythm — 'Love — love fades away. But things... Things are forever.' — has a deliberate, pseudo-profound cadence that makes it quotable and hilarious. The pause before 'Things' is a structural masterpiece. Earns its 8+ by being simultaneously deeply Tom-specific and universally funny as an inversion of wedding clichés.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at this! A serrated bread knife with an ergonomic grip. We NEED this.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we already have three bread knives.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not like this one, we don't. And actually, we need TWO of these. One for bread, one for... other breads.

jokes.text: Did the Dalai Lama say that?
jokes.setup: Tom has just said 'Things are forever' with complete sincerity.
jokes.punchline: Ben's straight-faced question treats Tom's consumerist platitude as potentially profound — the joke being that it's so confidently delivered it almost sounds like wisdom.
jokes.explanation: A great button on joke #8. Ben playing it completely straight amplifies Tom's absurdity. The Dalai Lama reference elevates the non-sequitur to spiritual territory.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We could sell naming rights to park features. You know, 'The Sweetums Bench,' 'The Paunch Burger Gazebo.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's actually a great idea, Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We could sell naming rights to anything. 'The JJ's Diner Drinking Fountain,' 'The Kwame Jackson Trashcan.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ooh, what about 'The Rent-A-Swag Tree'?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Sure. 'The Sweetums Ant Colony.' 'The Paunch Burger Air.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're not naming the air, Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: Ooh! A citrus reamer! Oh, this is the only way to ream citrus. You're gonna need two of these.
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are discussing the serious problem of the park funding shortfall at the registry.
jokes.punchline: Tom is completely oblivious to the crisis, rapturously excited about a kitchen tool, and insisting they need two.
jokes.explanation: Tom's selective focus — excited about 'reaming citrus' while a crisis unfolds — is solid character comedy. 'The only way to ream citrus' has an unintentionally suggestive quality that adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: These are Egyptian cotton sheets. 1,200 thread count. I had them specially ordered from a supplier in Cairo.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't believe in romance, but I do believe in high-quality linens.

jokes.text: I don't want a citrus reamer. I don't want any of this stuff. Look, all I want is to be married to you and to somehow get $50,000.
jokes.setup: Tom is extolling registry items; the audience expects Leslie to engage with wedding planning.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's priorities strip away the romantic moment — marriage and $50,000 in the same breath, delivered with total earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie — the romantic and the bureaucratic are completely fused in her mind. The specificity of '$50,000' alongside 'married to you' makes it land harder than a vague reference to work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, applaud.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no, no, no. Why are you applauding? I didn't say anything yet.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is exactly like when my kids clap before I finish the sentence. I hate that.

jokes.text: Right, some of that is possible.
jokes.setup: Leslie proposes naming rights for benches, cobblestones, trees, ants, and air.
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'some of that is possible' gently acknowledges that several of Leslie's ideas are insane while not wanting to crush her enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — Ben's diplomatic understatement does a lot of work in five words. The contrast between Leslie's escalating list (ants, air) and Ben's measured response is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, can you handle the vendors?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Sure, I'll make sure everything is on a roll.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Please don't.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I'll ketchup with them later.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, stop.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is going to be egg-cellent. I mean, lettuce be honest, I'm on a roll. Lettuce, get it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm walking away now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not even going to say I'm the cream of the crop? Because I'm dairy good at this.

jokes.text: Hey, guys. I'm really feeling these sheets — very cozy.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben have just had a creative breakthrough and rush off excitedly.
jokes.punchline: Tom is still browsing the registry, completely unaware the conversation has ended, blissfully absorbed in thread count.
jokes.explanation: A scene-ending tag that works because of timing — Tom talking to nobody while genuinely moved by bedsheets. Functional comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Fine, fine. I'll stop with the food puns. I guess you could say I'm going cold turkey.

jokes.text: Well, if I told you to jump off a bridge, would you do it? I hope so, because the only way that this gala is going to happen is if you do everything I say.
jokes.setup: Leslie chides the team for applauding when she told them to, using the classic parental rhetorical question.
jokes.punchline: She immediately subverts the expected answer ('No, you shouldn't!') by saying she HOPES they would, reframing the cliché into an authoritarian management style.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection on a familiar setup. The audience anticipates the standard punchline and Leslie completely inverts it. It's also deeply in character — Leslie's benevolent dictatorship framed as encouragement. The structure is tight and the subversion is genuinely surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh no, oh no, oh no! My family! I have to call my family!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Jerry, it's just a drill.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: A drill?! Well why didn't you say so! Phew!

jokes.text: Tom's food pun sequence: 'I'm omelet.' / 'Good-pie.' / 'Gurt. Go-gurt. I'm incredible.'
jokes.setup: Leslie assigns Tom a task and tells him to get going.
jokes.punchline: Tom responds with 'I'm omelet' (on it), then 'Good-pie' (goodbye), then keeps going with 'Gurt. Go-gurt. I'm incredible.' — the escalation into nonsense and self-congratulation is the peak.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from a functional pun ('omelet') to a weaker one ('good-pie') to a complete non-sequitur ('Gurt. Go-gurt.') followed by genuine self-satisfaction is perfectly constructed. Leslie's 'I get it, and I love it, but I don't have time for food puns right now' is a great straight-man line, and Tom pushing past it into nonsense makes it a mini-escalation arc.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's just a drill.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have to admit, I do enjoy the fake chaos.

jokes.text: On last year's report, they stated, 'Every time it so much as drizzles in Pawnee, the town is in danger of collapsing into Thunderdome-style, post-apocalyptic mayhem.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains that Pawnee has failed the emergency preparedness drill 12 years in a row.
jokes.punchline: The official government report using 'Thunderdome-style, post-apocalyptic mayhem' is the joke — bureaucratic language colliding with apocalyptic imagery, plus the specificity of 'it so much as drizzles.'
jokes.explanation: The incongruity of a government document citing Mad Max: Beyond Thunderdome is funny world-building. 'It so much as drizzles' compounds it by making the trigger absurdly minor against the apocalyptic consequence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: According to Pawnee's emergency preparedness report, a light drizzle is comparable to a Mad Max-level societal collapse.

jokes.text: I feel like I'm gonna nail [the personality evaluation], 'cause people always say, 'But he's got a great personality.'
jokes.setup: Andy says he'll nail the personality test because people always say he has a great personality.
jokes.punchline: The word 'but' implies people are saying his personality compensates for something — he's quoting a backhanded compliment as if it were unconditional praise.
jokes.explanation: This is layered and brilliant. Andy's obliviousness to the implicit slight in 'but he's got a great personality' is perfect character work — he hears only the compliment, not the concession. The joke requires no explanation to land but rewards attention. High character integration (only Andy) and excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Help! Someone help me! Margaret! Margaret!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Should we do something?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, he seems to be handling it.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm having a heart attack! Margaret!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: He's definitely panicking.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, but is it our problem?

jokes.text: What is the criminal code for a 3542? / Assault and battery. The way I remember that, I picture 35 salt shakers and 42 batteries.
jokes.setup: April quizzes Andy on police codes; he gives the correct answer.
jokes.punchline: His mnemonic — picturing 35 salt shakers and 42 batteries — is completely irrational as a memory device but stated with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Andy's absurd mnemonic works because (a) it's completely useless as a memory device, (b) he's clearly proud of it, and (c) the literalism of splitting the numbers — 35 shakers, 42 batteries — shows he's put real thought into this nonsensical system. Sets up the callback joke perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not worried about the personality evaluation. I'm very confident in my personality.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: People are always telling me, 'You have such a great personality.'

jokes.text: Arson is 533. You know how I remember that? I picture 533 salt shakers and batteries lighting a building on fire.
jokes.setup: Joke #18 established Andy's salt-shaker/battery mnemonic.
jokes.punchline: He applies the same logic to arson — now using a combined 533 objects, and they're 'lighting a building on fire.' The callback escalates the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The callback lands harder than the original because the system is now established and he's faithfully applying it with zero self-awareness. The detail that the combined objects are now doing the arson (actively 'lighting a building on fire') rather than just existing as numbers is the twist that elevates this. One of the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So for assault, I picture a giant salt shaker. A-salt. Get it?

jokes.text: And if you don't [pass], I'll just divorce you and marry someone else and then cheat on them with you.
jokes.setup: April encouragingly tells Andy he'll pass his test, then offers a backup plan.
jokes.punchline: Her idea of romantic reassurance involves divorce and infidelity as expressions of devotion — classic April dark romance.
jokes.explanation: Only April could frame adultery as a love declaration. The structure — building to 'cheat on them with you' as the romantic payoff — is well-constructed, and Andy's 'Aw, that's so sweet' makes it land perfectly as a relationship-specific character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Now hundreds of salt shakers are committing arson in his mental image.

jokes.text: I found a dead rabbit on the side of the road, and I cut its feet off and made it into a lucky charm.
jokes.setup: April tells Andy she got him a lucky charm.
jokes.punchline: The 'lucky charm' is a DIY rabbit's foot sourced from roadkill — April's Gothic domesticity applied to a sweet gesture.
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — April doing something sweet in the most unsettling way possible. 'Baby, you are so creepy. Thank you. I love it.' from Andy perfectly mirrors his unconditional love of April's darkness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're going to do great on that test. And if you don't pass, I have a backup plan. I've already contacted three women from your high school and I'm working on a fourth. If you fail the police exam, you can move in with one of them, start a new family, and leave all this behind.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm being supportive. That's what you wanted, right?

jokes.text: My mother is getting a colonoscopy today. I'm not even sure there's anyone there to drive her home, so we're all making sacrifices.
jokes.setup: Leslie says the drill is inconvenient because of the gala.
jokes.punchline: Leonard one-ups her with his own sacrifice — a mother potentially stranded after a colonoscopy — delivered with complete bureaucratic equanimity.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'colonoscopy' and the detail about nobody being there to drive her home makes this land. The follow-up — 'We're not that close.' — is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: She made it by mutilating roadkill

jokes.text: Mm, we're not that close. / Oh. Good.
jokes.setup: Leslie expresses sympathy for Leonard's mother's colonoscopy situation.
jokes.punchline: Leonard reveals they're not close; Leslie's relieved 'Oh. Good.' is the perfect inappropriate response — she's just glad she doesn't have to feel bad.
jokes.explanation: Magnificent economy. Leslie's 'Oh. Good.' is one word too honest, landing as both a character moment (her pragmatism overcoming social grace) and a well-timed beat. The joke is entirely in that two-word response.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, this is the sweetest, creepiest thing anyone has ever done for me. Thank you.

jokes.text: Leonard attempts to start the drill countdown — goes past zero and has to wait for it to come back around.
jokes.setup: Leonard is about to start the drill with dramatic gravitas.
jokes.punchline: He fumbles the countdown timer, goes past zero, and has to sheepishly wait for it to cycle back — undercutting all his authority.
jokes.explanation: Classic authority-puncturing physical comedy. The bureaucratic villain who can't work his own timer is a solid visual gag. Not particularly original but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: I had to leave my mother's deathbed to be here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Don't be. She was a real bitch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Wait. Maybe this is a nightmare. [Beat.] Nope, can't fly away. This is real life.
jokes.setup: Leslie is stuck in lockdown during the most important day of her event planning life.
jokes.punchline: She tests whether she's dreaming by trying to fly — a completely earnest use of dream logic — and concludes with matter-of-fact certainty: 'This is real life.'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. The joke works on multiple levels: Leslie's earnestness (she genuinely tries to fly), the absurdist logic (flying as nightmare diagnosis), and the deadpan conclusion ('This is real life'). It's original, perfectly structured as a beat, deeply character-specific — Leslie is someone who would absolutely test dream physics with total seriousness — and deeply quotable. One of the episode's best moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Alright everyone, gather around. I'm about to say something very important.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Wait, my stopwatch... hold on.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Okay, starting over. Alright everyone, gather around. I'm about to say something very important.

jokes.text: Yes! Avian flu! Jackpot.
jokes.setup: The disaster scenario is opened — Leslie anxiously awaits a complicated scenario.
jokes.punchline: Avian flu is apparently a relief — Leslie treats 'jackpot' as unironic because she has a prepared protocol for it. The audience laughs at her warped priority system.
jokes.explanation: Only Leslie would feel lucky to get avian flu. Her preparedness obsession turned a public health catastrophe into a winning lottery ticket. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, if this is a nightmare, I should be able to fly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm gonna jump off this desk and fly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Nope. Still on the ground. This is real.

jokes.text: That's 'Mission Im-Pawnee-able: Knope Protocol.'
jokes.setup: Someone calls it 'The Knope Protocol.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie corrects them with the full title — a pun on Mission: Impossible combined with Pawnee's name, plus her own name. Three layers of self-branding in a crisis protocol.
jokes.explanation: The pun is good but the real joke is Leslie's brand management even during emergencies. Three layers of self-reference packed into a government protocol name.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: We've been hit by avian flu.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jackpot! Do you know how easy avian flu is to handle? It's just birds. We don't even like birds. They're basically dinosaurs that never evolved.

jokes.text: Ron volunteers for TV: 'I can speak in full sentences, and I won't cry.' / 'Fair point. I did cry last time.'
jokes.setup: The team needs someone to sub for Leslie on a TV appearance; concern is raised about Ron.
jokes.punchline: Ron's qualifications for television are hilariously minimal ('full sentences, won't cry'), and Ben's concession — 'I did cry last time' — validates them completely.
jokes.explanation: The two-beat structure is tight: Ron's impossibly low bar for competence, followed by Ben accepting it because his own bar was apparently even lower. Both characters are served well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not an emergency protocol, it's a disaster preparedness initiative. And it's called 'The Lesslie Knope Guide to Knope-ing with Disaster.' Get it? Knope? Like my last name? Because I'm hoping we can knope our way through any crisis.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've been working on that pun for three years.

jokes.text: Great leadership -- inspiring.
jokes.setup: Donna calls Leslie about chair shortages; Leslie says 'get some chairs from somewhere.'
jokes.punchline: Tom's sarcastic 'Great leadership — inspiring' undercuts Leslie's vague directive with deadpan disdain.
jokes.explanation: A quick sarcasm beat. Functional but not especially crafted — standard deflation of authority.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Hello, I'm Dr. Donna Meagle, MD, PhD, DDS, and several other letters.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I've been practicing emergency medicine for over forty years, and I've saved thousands of lives.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm also a world-renowned surgeon, an acclaimed chef, and I speak seventeen languages fluently.

jokes.text: Little coq au vin? Little bouillabaisse? / You can stop the ass-kissing, Haverford.
jokes.setup: Tom approaches the chef trying to get free catering.
jokes.punchline: Tom's fawning culinary name-dropping is immediately seen through — 'You can stop the ass-kissing' — before he's even made his ask.
jokes.explanation: Tom's transparent strategy and the chef's instant dismissal is a reliable comedy structure. The French dish name-dropping is in character.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That was the most inspiring delegation I've ever heard. I'm going to go start a small business based solely on that speech.

jokes.text: Doesn't that offend your refined Parisian sensibilities? / I'm from Orlando.
jokes.setup: Tom tries to appeal to the chef's French cultural pride.
jokes.punchline: The chef is from Orlando — completely deflating Tom's sophisticated appeal.
jokes.explanation: The economy is excellent — 'I'm from Orlando' does maximum damage in minimum words, obliterating Tom's entire angle. Classic misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would never cry on television.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I have. Multiple times. It's not something I'm proud of, but it happened.

jokes.text: And I don't care about the Paunch Burger. If it was another French restaurant, maybe I'd worry.
jokes.setup: Tom argues the chef should care about Paunch Burger opening nearby.
jokes.punchline: The chef's only concern would be competition from another French restaurant — not a fast food chain, revealing his professional insularity.
jokes.explanation: A decent character-specific joke — the chef's snobbery cuts both ways (he's dismissive of fast food but also from Orlando). Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm appealing to your refined Parisian sensibilities.

dialogue.speaker: Chef
dialogue.line: I'm from Orlando. I only care about French competition cooking shows.

jokes.text: Tom is chased out of the kitchen by an angry chef screaming 'Get out of my kitchen! / Pardon! Pardon!'
jokes.setup: Tom has pushed the chef too far.
jokes.punchline: Tom's retreat involves shouting 'Pardon! Pardon!' — attempting French politeness while being physically ejected.
jokes.explanation: Tom's use of the one French word he knows while being thrown out is a nice character touch. The physical comedy is inferred but the dialogue rhythm suggests chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, pardon, pardon!

dialogue.speaker: Chef
dialogue.line: Get out!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Pardon! Je suis désolé! I apologize!

dialogue.speaker: Chef
dialogue.line: OUT!

jokes.text: Leslie video-conferencing with Animal Control's Brett: 'Kill all birds.' / 'This is for the drill, right?' / 'Yes.' / 'But I'm actually gonna kill these birds for real?'
jokes.setup: Leslie gives Brett instructions to 'eradicate all infected birds' as part of the drill.
jokes.punchline: Brett confirms it's a drill but then immediately asks if he should still actually kill the birds — making the distinction between drill and reality meaningless to him.
jokes.explanation: Brett's complete inability to distinguish simulation from reality is good absurdist comedy. The logical paradox — it's a drill but he still plans to execute birds — escalates naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Au revoir, chef! C'est la vie!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Bon appétit! Je m'en vais!

jokes.text: I could fill up a bathtub and just drown 'em one at a time. / Okay, let's forget we ever talked. / Got it. Kill 'em.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to back away from the bird-killing conversation.
jokes.punchline: Brett's DIY drowning solution, Leslie's attempt to pretend it never happened, and Brett's cheerful 'Got it. Kill 'em.' — he has completely misunderstood the backpedal.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'kill the birds' to 'bathtub drowning one at a time' to 'Got it. Kill 'em.' is a perfect three-beat absurdist gag. Leslie's attempt to retract and Brett gleefully confirming the original order is a great structural reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying you want me to pretend to kill birds? Like, what does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, just act it out. Pretend you're hunting them.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Okay, so I could use a gun? Or maybe set traps? What about poison? I could poison them. Or use my bare hands and strangle them one by one. I could build a giant bird cage and slowly starve them. I could—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay! Just... just pretend to shoo them away or something.

jokes.text: A few months ago, the thought of an infectious disease, even hypothetical, would have sent me careening towards Bummerville, but now I am infected with a killer virus, and I feel fine. Therapy!
jokes.setup: Chris has been designated 'infected' in the drill.
jokes.punchline: Chris turns his simulated death sentence into a testament to therapy, culminating in the single-word triumph: 'Therapy!'
jokes.explanation: 'Bummerville' as Chris's term for depression is great character vocabulary. The pivot to 'Therapy!' as a one-word victory shout is highly quotable and perfectly in character for the relentlessly positive Chris Traeger.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, this is a drill. We're pretending to kill the birds.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Pretending?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, Brett. It's a drill.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Oh, because I've been actually killing them.

jokes.text: I do not ride the bus. I ride my bicycle behind the bus as a windbreak.
jokes.setup: Leonard tells Chris he rode the bus and infected 39 people.
jokes.punchline: Chris's correction reveals an even stranger behavior — drafting behind a bus on a bicycle — delivered as if this is completely normal and should satisfy Leonard's objection.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Chris tries to correct a factual error but reveals something far weirder — bicycle drafting behind a bus as a fitness optimization. It's deeply original, perfectly in character (Chris's insane health regime), economically delivered, and earns its laugh entirely from character logic rather than a cheap twist. 'Windbreak' is the perfect word choice. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Let's not talk about this anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Okay, so we're doing this. I'll get the shotgun.

jokes.text: Doesn't matter. Prepare for the diarrhea.
jokes.setup: Chris protests the bus-riding logic.
jokes.punchline: Leonard dismisses the argument entirely with a clinical, emotionless warning about imminent diarrhea.
jokes.explanation: Four words. Maximum impact. 'Prepare for the diarrhea' is delivered with the gravity of a death sentence by a bureaucrat who has done this a thousand times. The contrast between the clinical tone and the undignified subject matter is perfectly calibrated. Highly quotable in isolation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're doing well with low casualties.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Actually, Chris Pratt is now infected.

jokes.text: My bad, guys. That's my bad. / Damn it, Jamm. / I should've had animal control kill you. / Oh, who you want me to kill? / No one. / I'll kill him... As soon as I'm done with these birds.
jokes.setup: Jamm is revealed as responsible for the bus protocol failure. Brett — still on the bird-killing task — checks in.
jokes.punchline: Brett's cheerful willingness to add murder to his task list, and his responsible prioritization of finishing the birds first, is the callback payoff.
jokes.explanation: The callback earns its place because Brett's priorities — finishing the birds before committing murder, as if both are equivalent tasks — is perfect absurdist logic. The efficiency of 'As soon as I'm done with these birds' is great.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, I've been exposed to a deadly virus and I'm not panicking? This is huge! Do you know what this means? I'm finally emotionally stable!

jokes.text: I went on a booze cruise last week. It just finished up an hour ago. On a completely unrelated note, I have horrible allergies.
jokes.setup: Joan is clearly suffering from a terrible hangover as Ron arrives for his TV appearance.
jokes.punchline: Joan's alibi — 'completely unrelated' allergies — immediately follows the explanation that she was on a week-long booze cruise that ended an hour ago.
jokes.explanation: The transparent self-deception of 'completely unrelated' is a reliable comedy device, elevated here by the extreme specificity of 'a booze cruise that just ended an hour ago.' Joan's denial is proportional to the evidence against it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I wasn't on the bus. I was cycling behind it the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You were... cycling behind the bus?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's called drafting. It's very efficient. The bus breaks the wind resistance, and I just follow along at a safe distance.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Chris, that might be the weirdest thing you've ever done, and you once ate a whole rotisserie chicken in the park at 6 AM.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That was different. That was about protein optimization.

jokes.text: Hello. I'm Joan Callamezzo. Today's show will not go on.
jokes.setup: The classic 'the show must go on' declaration was just made; Joan counts down dramatically.
jokes.punchline: The immediate inversion — 'Today's show will not go on' — delivered in her anchor voice as she collapses from her hangover.
jokes.explanation: A perfect subversion of the 'show must go on' setup, delivered in Joan's professional anchor cadence which makes the collapse even funnier. The structure — anticipation built by the count-in, then complete opposite of expected — is textbook misdirection with excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I should have had you killed.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: I can do that. I'll get to it right after I feed the birds.

jokes.text: Ron Swanson on live TV: 'My name is Ron Swanson. I am here to tell you about a black-tie gala fund-raiser for Pawnee Commons happening tonight. All proceeds will go toward building a park. It will be enjoyable.'
jokes.setup: Ron, a man who hates publicity and government, has been thrust onto live television to promote a civic event.
jokes.punchline: 'It will be enjoyable' — the most minimal, low-enthusiasm endorsement possible from someone who communicates in terse facts.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Ron's version of a promotional appearance strips away every convention of salesmanship — no enthusiasm, no superlatives, just a terse recitation of facts ending with 'It will be enjoyable.' The gap between what television promotion requires and what Ron can deliver is enormous, and the joke fully exploits it. 'It will be enjoyable' is perfectly Ron and perfectly deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I'm not feeling well.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I just got back from a week-long booze cruise.

jokes.text: Take a — take a phone call. / Now I will take your calls, apparently.
jokes.setup: Ron finishes his prepared statement and is evidently told by producers to take calls.
jokes.punchline: 'Now I will take your calls, apparently' — Ron announces this as if mildly put-upon, treating the normal format of a call-in show as an imposition.
jokes.explanation: 'Apparently' does all the work — it signals Ron's reluctant compliance with a format he doesn't understand or endorse. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: It's not a hangover, it's allergies.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Joan, you just got back from a week-long booze cruise.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Yes, and I have allergies. Two unrelated things.

jokes.text: Caller asks Joan to settle a bet about 'the sexiest couple in history — R-Patz and K-Stew, or Bieber—' [Joan passes out]
jokes.setup: Ron is attempting to field calls about the gala; instead the callers are asking Joan their usual pop-culture questions.
jokes.punchline: Joan collapses mid-question — her hangover finally winning — cutting off the caller at the most inane possible moment.
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy payoff. The inanity of the question ('R-Patz and K-Stew') makes Joan's collapse feel like a mercy, and the cut-off timing is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: The show must go on!

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Actually, the show is over. Everyone go home.

jokes.text: It seems like her allergies are kicking in.
jokes.setup: Joan has visibly collapsed from her hangover on live television.
jokes.punchline: Ben's straight-faced callback to Joan's cover story — 'allergies' — as if the official narrative must be maintained.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback button — maintaining the fiction with complete deadpan. Economy is good but the joke is fairly predictable once the allergies cover story was established.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.line: Joan, I have a serious relationship question.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Of course, what is it?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.line: Do you think Zayn and Harry are still together, or is Zarry over?

jokes.text: Personality test scenario: 'Your name is Andy?' / 'I don't know how to answer that. Well, everyone calls me Andy, but my full name is Andrew, I think, so... No? Wait. Yes.'
jokes.setup: A calibration question on the personality test — 'Is your name Andy?' — designed to have an obvious answer.
jokes.punchline: Andy overthinks it into genuine uncertainty about his own identity, including 'I think' about his legal name.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character moment. Only Andy could fail a calibration question about his own name. The detail of 'I think' regarding his full name suggests genuine uncertainty about basic biographical facts. The escalation through 'No? Wait. Yes.' perfectly mimics Andy's thought process. This is why he fails the personality test — not stupidity exactly, but a unique relationship with basic reality.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we have a problem. The caterer double-booked us, the band cancelled, and Jerry somehow got locked in the storage closet during setup.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry? Again? How is that even possible?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't know, but that's not even the worst part. We've been looking for him for hours. We declared a fake emergency to search the building.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And Jerry is still missing.

jokes.text: Scenario: A high-school-aged child asks to hold your service revolver. What do you do? / 'Yes, I give it to him. When I was a kid, I always wanted to hold a cop's gun. To make that dream come true for another kid — well, that's what being a cop is all about.'
jokes.setup: A test scenario about refusing to give your weapon to a child.
jokes.punchline: Andy not only gives the child the gun but frames it as the philosophical core of police work — making children's dreams come true.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. Andy's answer isn't stupidity — it's sincere, earnest good intentions applied catastrophically incorrectly. 'That's what being a cop is all about' reframes dangerous negligence as noble idealism, which is both funnier and sadder than simple ignorance. The structure (wrong answer → heartfelt justification → even wronger philosophical conclusion) is perfect escalation. The character integration is total — only Andy reasons this way.

dialogue.speaker: Examiner
dialogue.line: Your name is Andy, correct?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, it depends on how you define 'is.' I mean, technically my birth certificate says Andrew, but everyone calls me Andy. So is Andy really my name, or is Andrew my name and Andy is just what people call me? And honestly, some days I don't even feel like an Andy. Some days I feel more like a... I don't know, a Derek?

jokes.text: You pull over your father for speeding. How do you handle it? / 'Well, first I would be like, Dad... You're alive? What the hell? Also, do you know where my catcher's mitt is?'
jokes.setup: A standard police ethics scenario about nepotism.
jokes.punchline: Andy's father is apparently dead (or abandoned him), turning a simple ethics question into an unexpected emotional revelation — followed immediately by asking about a catcher's mitt.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode by a significant margin. The question expects a cop-ethics answer; instead we get an unexpected family tragedy AND comedy simultaneously. 'You're alive? What the hell?' alone would be a great joke, but 'Also, do you know where my catcher's mitt is?' is transcendent — the mundane grievance about a childhood possession immediately after existential shock captures Andy's emotional range perfectly. It's funny, sad, deeply character-specific, and completely unpredictable. The structure is exceptional: setup (ethics question) → misdirection (dead dad reveal) → escalation (catcher's mitt). Approaches the calibration anchor level.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You don't want to let the kid hold the gun? That's like, the whole point of being a cop. That's police work right there.

jokes.text: Ron's live TV advice segment: hangover cure of flank steak, salted butter, wet socks, sleep.
jokes.setup: A caller asks about Joan's obvious hangover; Ron responds with his personal cure.
jokes.punchline: The cure is a large flank steak pan-fried in salted butter, followed by wet socks and sleep — Ron's caveman approach to medicine delivered with complete authority.
jokes.explanation: The wet socks detail elevates this from 'Ron eats steak' to something genuinely weird. The specificity — salted butter, wet socks — gives it the authority of folk medicine, which makes Ron's confidence even funnier. 'It does.' as a closing affirmation is perfectly Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, I can't pull over my dad for speeding.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My dad's dead.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Also, what's the difference between a baseball glove and a baseball mitt?

jokes.text: Ron's list of call-in interests: 'Woodworking, uh, novels about tall ships, meat, that sort of thing.'
jokes.setup: Ron redirects callers to the gala but offers alternative topics.
jokes.punchline: 'Novels about tall ships' and 'meat, that sort of thing' — Ron is essentially asking Pawnee viewers to call in about Ron Swanson interests on a local lifestyle show.
jokes.explanation: 'Novels about tall ships' is a perfect Ron Swanson detail — so specific, so him, so useless on a morning lifestyle show. The fact that he's advertising his personal interests instead of the gala is great character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She's a woman.

jokes.text: Chris reads his own death announcement: 'I, Chris Traeger, after several sustained hours of diarrhea, combined with violent coughing and a devastating fever, followed by even more diarrhea, have succumbed to the avian flu.' / 'I'm dead.'
jokes.setup: The drill simulation has progressed; Chris has been declared dead.
jokes.punchline: Chris reads his own death notice aloud with his characteristic positivity, then simply states 'I'm dead.' — the drama of the formal announcement punctured by his unperturbed delivery.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the diarrhea warning — now listed twice in the death notice — pays off the earlier joke. 'Followed by even more diarrhea' is a good escalation. Chris reading his own death announcement with cheerful professionalism is character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.line: Will Joan be okay?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Oh, she'll be fine. I never get hangovers.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The key is before you go to bed, you have to drink a glass of warm milk, do 50 push-ups, and think about Indians.

jokes.text: Councilman Jamm requested [the drill be done today] and said I should give you everything I got.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks why the drill is so unusually intensive.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Jamm orchestrated the entire disaster — turning Leonard from antagonist into unknowing weapon — recontextualizes the whole episode.
jokes.explanation: A plot reveal that functions as comedy through the recontextualization — Jamm's pettiness reaches new heights by weaponizing government bureaucracy. The rewatch bonus comes from understanding all of Leonard's sadism as Jamm's doing.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: In the event of my death, I want my remains to be cremated, and my ashes scattered in a place of natural beauty. However, if I am to die from a bizarre accident involving a drill, I accept that my final moments will be marked by a sudden onset of vertigo, followed by acute abdominal trauma, profuse hemorrhaging, loss of consciousness, and ultimately, catastrophic organ failure.

jokes.text: It is with a heavy heart that I say, 'We have been jammed.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals Jamm's sabotage to the team.
jokes.punchline: 'We have been jammed' — both the literal act (screwed over) and a pun on Jamm's name, delivered with Leslie's trademark formal gravity.
jokes.explanation: The formality of 'It is with a heavy heart' before a name-pun lands because Leslie can't help but make even casual wordplay sound like an official statement.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My interests are woodworking, fishing, hunting, carpentry, and the study of government.

jokes.text: In order to save our park... We have to destroy the entire town.
jokes.setup: Leslie rallies the team after discovering they've been sabotaged.
jokes.punchline: The heroic framing ('save our park') resolved by the most disproportionate solution possible ('destroy the entire town') — delivered as completely reasonable.
jokes.explanation: The strategic pivot from 'ace the test' to 'destroy the town' as a reasonable escalation of problem-solving is a great Leslie moment. The dramatic pause before 'We have to destroy the entire town' makes it land as a genuine action-hero beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Wait a minute... the timing of this intensive drill is awfully convenient.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard Huggins
dialogue.line: Yeah, about that... Jamm orchestrated the whole thing.

jokes.text: Tell the hospital director to flush all the flu vaccines down the toilet. / You got it. / Chief Fugleberg, order your officers to find all infected birds and perform CPR.
jokes.setup: Leslie implements her sabotage plan to fail the drill as spectacularly as possible.
jokes.punchline: Performing CPR on infected birds to save them — the opposite of the correct response — is the escalating absurdity of Leslie intentionally failing with the same competence she brings to succeeding.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Leslie applies the same thoroughness to failing as to succeeding. CPR on infected birds is specifically funny because it inverts both the birds-as-disease-vector logic and the cull-the-birds instinct simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We've been jammed.

jokes.text: Oh, no! Pawnee has been hit with... A tornado quake!
jokes.setup: Leslie is deliberately maximizing the disaster scenarios.
jokes.punchline: 'Tornado quake' — a portmanteau disaster that doesn't exist, Leslie apparently inventing new natural disasters on the fly.
jokes.explanation: Leslie stacking disasters compounds the absurdism nicely. 'Tornado quake' is the kind of thing a panicked government official would invent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I have a new strategy. We're going to dig ourselves out of this hole by digging an even bigger hole.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's what they said about the Internet, Ben. And look at us now.

jokes.text: I've seen three movies in my life — Bridge on the River Kwai, Patton, and Herbie Fully Loaded. My girlfriend's kids love it. It's pretty funny.
jokes.setup: Ron's call-in advice continues; he mentions movies unprompted.
jokes.punchline: Ron's three films are two serious war epics and Herbie Fully Loaded — the Disney racing car movie — with a genuine, warm endorsement: 'It's pretty funny.'
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The list of two prestigious war films is a perfect Ron setup — then Herbie Fully Loaded lands like a detonation. What makes it exceptional is 'My girlfriend's kids love it. It's pretty funny.' — Ron has seen this movie, evaluated it on his own terms, and genuinely endorses it. The humanity is the joke. It reveals Ron's softness without sentimentality, and the choice of Herbie Fully Loaded specifically (not a better kids' movie) is inspired. This nearly reaches the calibration anchor level.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're telling me we still have flu vaccine supplies left?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Destroy them. All of them. We need this crisis to be as bad as possible.

jokes.text: And... it is a wrap. Everyone in Pawnee is dead. Including Councilman Jamm.
jokes.setup: Leonard announces the end of the drill.
jokes.punchline: Specifically mentioning Jamm's fictional death — and the implication that he died in the disaster he engineered — is Leonard's small dry flourish.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of calling out Jamm's fictional death — out of all of Pawnee — shows Leonard has some awareness or satisfaction. A small but effective beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Orders to all units: we need you to perform CPR on any diseased birds you encounter in the park. This is a public health emergency.

jokes.text: What? No, no, you can't do that. / It says right there, you're dead, so is everyone you care about. / Oh, well, joke's on you. I don't have anyone I care about.
jokes.setup: Jamm protests his fictional death.
jokes.punchline: Jamm's attempted comeback — 'I don't have anyone I care about' — is meant as a power move but is actually a sad and revealing character confession.
jokes.explanation: The joke has depth — Jamm delivers this as a boast, but it's actually a tragic admission played completely straight by an oblivious villain. The joke functions on two levels simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I've got it. What if we had a torricane?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A tornado and a hurricane had a baby. It's a torricane. It has the unpredictability of a tornado with the destructive power of a hurricane.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not yet it isn't.

jokes.text: Thank you for your time. I think we're done here. I will see everyone at the gala, and I will see you in hell.
jokes.setup: Leslie graciously thanks Leonard despite failing the drill.
jokes.punchline: 'I will see everyone at the gala, and I will see you in hell' — transitioning from professional courtesy to genuine damnation in a single sentence.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from event promotion to damnation in one sentence, delivered with identical professional smoothness, is great Leslie. The structure — public announcement → sudden personal vendetta — is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.line: How do I repair dog damage to my furniture?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: There are several options. You can use wood filler for small scratches, or refinish the entire piece. Alternatively, you could get rid of the dog.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.line: I love my dog though.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Then I suggest a more permanent solution: eliminate all small dogs.

jokes.text: I can't hear you. I'm a ghost. / Yeah, well, so am I, so you can hear me! / Ghost jammed!
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to dismiss Jamm; he insists she can hear him.
jokes.punchline: 'Ghost jammed!' — Jamm's victory cry for winning a ghost-logic argument is both absurd (ghost rules applied seriously) and another Jamm name-pun.
jokes.explanation: The absurdist ghost logic debate is funny on its own, but 'Ghost jammed!' — Jamm's self-branding applied to a supernatural context — is delightful. It commits fully to the bit and rewards Jamm with a genuine win using his own linguistic vanity.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Banks? They're just fancy legalized theft operations run by people in suits who are too cowardly to actually rob you themselves. At least a common criminal has the decency to be honest about what he's doing.

jokes.text: We got all the way to Muncie before we realized it was just a drill. All I'm saying is you could've called. / No one had your cell number, Big 'J.' / I find that hard to believe.
jokes.setup: Jerry reappears after being missing the entire episode.
jokes.punchline: 'No one had your cell number, Big J' — a plausible but clearly pretextual excuse that everyone uses to leave Jerry out, which he half-believes anyway.
jokes.explanation: A classic Jerry running gag — he was genuinely abandoned and the team's excuse is transparently implausible. 'Big J' from Ben is an unexpected affectionate nickname that makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Look, I don't care about your business complications. Capitalism is simple: I give you money, you give me a thing. That's it. No committees, no forms, no women.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, I destroyed the entire town for nothing.
jokes.setup: Leslie sees the gala is somehow already set up despite her absence.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's summary of her day — 'I destroyed the entire town for nothing' — delivered as genuine regret about a government simulation.
jokes.explanation: The callback to her own battle cry is well-placed. The specificity of 'for nothing' as her primary concern — not the ethical dimension of simulated mass death — is character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've only seen two movies in my life. Saving Private Ryan and Apocalypse Now. Both of them are masterpieces.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The third movie I saw was a children's comedy. And I genuinely enjoyed it.

jokes.text: Who has the most to lose from a new Paunch Burger? Their competitors. I got all the other fast-food places in town to donate food.
jokes.setup: Leslie is amazed the gala has food despite nothing going to plan.
jokes.punchline: Tom's business insight — getting Paunch Burger's fast food competitors to supply a black-tie gala — is genuinely clever, but the result is finger food at a formal event.
jokes.explanation: Tom's solution is clever enough to be genuinely impressive, which makes it funny — he succeeded through shrewd logic, not in spite of it. 'Black tie and chicky tenders' as an aesthetic pairing is a nice detail.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Everyone in town is dead.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: That's not true! I have no loved ones to lose!

jokes.text: I know black tie and chicky tenders isn't the best mix, but — / No, Tom, I love it. And more importantly, so will all of our more ample citizens.
jokes.setup: Tom apologizes for the mismatch of formal gala and fast food.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'more ample citizens' — a politically diplomatic euphemism for overweight Pawnee residents who love fast food — delivered completely without irony.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's concern for Pawnee's obese population as a constituency is a running series joke, and 'more ample citizens' as a diplomatic phrasing she's clearly thought about is in character.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Well, if you're a ghost, then you can't hear the living world, right? So anything I say right now doesn't count as harassment!

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Treat yo' self!

jokes.text: I also helped a child perform a tracheotomy on his elderly uncle. It's been a very rewarding day.
jokes.setup: The team recaps their contributions to the gala.
jokes.punchline: Ron casually mentions performing emergency surgery on a child's uncle — a completely disproportionate achievement mentioned alongside 'went on TV' — as 'very rewarding.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. Ron's casual inclusion of supervising emergency surgery alongside his other achievements, delivered in the same tone as 'I went on TV,' is pitch-perfect deadpan. 'It's been a very rewarding day' as a button is magnificent — Ron's satisfaction is entirely genuine and entirely disproportionate to normal human experience. The specificity (child, tracheotomy, elderly uncle) adds absurd detail. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I drove all the way to Shelbyville before I realized it was a false alarm!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Jerry, you drove to another city?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, nobody told me it was fake! If you're going to have an emergency evacuation, maybe use the phone tree or send an email or something!

jokes.text: Oh, and thanks for dressing up, Jerry.
jokes.setup: The gala begins; everyone is in black tie.
jokes.punchline: Leslie specifically singles out Jerry for thanks — implying he's somehow embarrassingly overdressed or underdressed, or simply that thanking Jerry for basic compliance is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: The rewatch bonus applies because seeing what Jerry is wearing presumably makes this land much harder. As a transcript joke, it's solid but incomplete — the visual is doing heavy lifting we can't assess.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I solved the food problem. I went to all the competitors and I asked them if they wanted to sell me their food at a discount. They said yes. Boom. Genius.

jokes.text: He got 100% on his written test — first guy in history to do it — but he failed his personality examination. He's a sweet kid, just doesn't have what it takes to be a cop.
jokes.setup: We learn Andy's test results as we watch him doing a wrist-lock demonstration on himself.
jokes.punchline: 100% on the written test (unprecedented) but failed personality — the exact inverse of what his scenes showed us. The visual of Andy demonstrating police holds on himself simultaneously illustrates why.
jokes.explanation: The reveal works because we've watched Andy demonstrate both capacities simultaneously — his mnemonic system was clearly effective, while his actual judgment was catastrophic. 'First guy in history' is both a compliment and a setup for the contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I solved the catering problem by negotiating with three different vendors, playing them against each other, and leveraging my relationships to get a 40% discount. Some people call it business savvy. I call it the Tom Haverford special.

jokes.text: Official police wrist lock. You can't hit me. Try to hit me. Or here, no, try — it's this hand. Wrist lock. Boom, too much pain, you can't even hit me. Try to hit me. If I had my gun, you wouldn't try to hit me, though, is the thing.
jokes.setup: Andy has failed his test and is demonstrating police techniques at the gala.
jokes.punchline: Andy's wrist-lock demonstration keeps going wrong — he can't find the right hand, his technique is uncertain — and he resolves it by wishing he had a gun, which is its own problem.
jokes.explanation: Andy's gun comment ('if I had my gun') callbacks his earlier test answer about giving guns to children, making this funnier in retrospect. The physical fumbling is presumably charming to watch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I helped perform emergency surgery this morning. Then I went to the dentist.

jokes.text: Too bad. He's certainly something of a genius. We could use his brains on the force.
jokes.setup: Fugleberg observes Andy fumbling the wrist lock and wishing he had a gun.
jokes.punchline: Fugleberg, having just watched this, still calls Andy 'something of a genius' — the test results completely override observable reality in his assessment.
jokes.explanation: The irony is solid — the evidence of Andy's practical incompetence is happening in real time while Fugleberg praises his test scores. Works as an ironic counterpoint.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, I just want to say thank you for cleaning up and wearing formal attire tonight. You look very handsome.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, thank you Leslie. Though I have to admit, after the day I've had, I'm not entirely sure this tuxedo is appropriate anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you mean? You look perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I spent the last four hours running through the woods, fell into a creek, and got chased by what I'm pretty sure was a bear. So technically, this tuxedo is now a wetsuit.

jokes.text: Have you ever thought of being a sperm donor? / I'm impotent. / Yeah, I don't need to know that.
jokes.setup: Leslie thanks Leonard for reconsidering the drill grade; she's impressed by him.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's flattery leads to a completely unexpected and overshared personal medical detail — Leonard is impotent — followed by Leslie's retreat.
jokes.explanation: Three beats, perfectly efficient: Leslie's surprisingly forward question → Leonard's devastating personal overshare → Leslie's pragmatic withdrawal. The question itself is already a great Leslie-ism (she's thinking about civic utility, not flirting), which makes his answer even more surprising and her reaction ('I don't need to know that') funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Police Chief
dialogue.line: Andy aced the academic portion but failed the personality test completely.

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie decide to get married tonight at the gala, spontaneously, in front of all their friends.
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie note they're surrounded by everyone they know, in black tie, with food and entertainment.
jokes.punchline: The gala accidentally meets all the requirements for their wedding, so why not? The comedic logic (convenience as a reason to get married right now) is sweet and absurd.
jokes.explanation: More sweet than funny, but the comedic logic — 'we have all the ingredients, why not just do it?' — has an absurdist spontaneity that works. The rewatch bonus is high for series fans.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so when you fail, you gotta just shake it off. Like this.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You do a little spin, you take a deep breath, and then you just... move on to the next thing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's what we do in the Police Academy. Well, actually, we do a lot of things with guns.

jokes.text: The in-universe disaster DVD segments: 'Donatella Breckinridge, M.D.' and 'Jessica Rabrit' as the news anchor name.
jokes.setup: The drill uses a pre-recorded DVD of fake local news coverage.
jokes.punchline: 'Jessica Rabrit' as the anchor name — a thin disguise for 'Rabbit' that the show's fake local news always has absurd names. 'Donatella Breckinridge, M.D.' sounds deliberately over-credentialed.
jokes.explanation: Background comedy that rewards attentive viewing but isn't laugh-out-loud. The fake names are a consistent background gag in Parks & Rec.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leonard, can I ask you something personal?

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: The tornado quake disaster DVD: 'Isabella Winchester — celebrated geologist' / 'That's correct. It was a large one.'
jokes.setup: The fake news coverage of a tornado quake cuts to a geological expert.
jokes.punchline: 'That's correct. It was a large one.' — the geologist's expert analysis is hilariously minimal, confirming only what the anchor already said.
jokes.explanation: The expert adding nothing to the coverage while being identified as 'celebrated' is a nice media satire beat. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Ron, how often do you and Tammy have relations?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's... that's not something I'm going to discuss with you, Leonard.

jokes.text: The news anchor's name is 'Jessica Rabrit' — a near-homophone of Jessica Rabbit.
jokes.setup: The closing segment of the drill DVD has an anchor signing off.
jokes.punchline: Her name is 'Jessica Rabrit' — clearly a joke name, almost certainly a Jessica Rabbit reference.
jokes.explanation: A background joke that rewards attentive viewers. The Jessica Rabbit reference is mild but charming. Mostly a rewatch joke for people who catch the name on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to set a date. When do you want to get married?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't know, maybe next spring? We could do something really nice, plan it out properly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Next spring? Ben, I want to marry you now!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we can't just get married at the gala tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because... okay, you know what? Let's do it. Let's get married tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Really. I don't want to wait another day.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben organize a black tie gala to raise money for their park, but their plans are derailed when a city-wide emergency response drill is called. Meanwhile, Andy prepares to take his Police Academy Exam and Ron fills in for Leslie on Pawnee Today.
insight: Absurdist escalation drives a mid-tier entry: 76 jokes in 27 minutes, no standout moments.
